words.lemma: oíche (OIr. adaig), dat. sg. after de

cognate: The night-member only: ON nætr (acc. pl. of nátt/nótt) ~ Gk νύκτα/νύξ (Homeric νύκτας) ~ Lat. noctes ~ Ved. náktam, all < *nókʷt-. The day-member is renewed in every branch (ON dagr, Gk ἦμαρ/ἡμέρα, Lat. dies, Ved. dívā), so the cognate material is half the figure.
drift_or_renewal: Day-word renewed everywhere. The Irish member renews both words (lá, oidhche) and reverses the order (day first), following Latin die ac nocte in a translated Christian setting. Plato's anchor is also day-first and nominative, so it witnesses the pairing but not the archaic order or case.
shared_syntax: Coordinated merism of the night-word and a day-word used as an adverbial accusative of extent of time ('through nights and days', i.e. continuously) attached to a verb of motion or sustained activity. The night-word comes first and is plural in ON (nætr ok daga), Homer (νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ), Latin (noctes diesque) and is in the accusative in Vedic náktam. The ON slab anchor fits this exactly: riðr ... bæði nætr oc ðaga, 'rides after them both nights and days'. The Galen/Damocrates verse anchor has night-first accusative of duration (νύκτα ... ἡμέραν μίαν), but for a measured interval. The Plato anchor is only a list of time-divisions (ἡμέρα τε καὶ νὺξ).
context: ON Þiðreks saga (HolmPerg 4 fol; translated from Low German material): a king pursues with all his knights nights and days. Galen quoting Damocrates' iambic recipe: soak a night and a day. Plato Timaeus: day and night, months and years as the source of number. Irish (Keating-era devotional prose, nc): a woman prays to God by day and by night, weeping. The congruent comparison is with the corpus witnesses rather than the slab Greek: Homeric πλέομεν νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ 'we sailed nights and day' ~ saga siglðu þeir þá bæði nætr ok daga 'they sailed both nights and days'. Both have a voyage verb, the accusative of duration and night first. Homeric κλαύσονται νύκτας τε καὶ ἤματα 'they will weep nights and days' ~ the Irish weeping-and-praying setting, which is renewed and day-first. Why not just generic: the plural, night-first form is the marked one where a branch also has a day-first variant. ON singular dag ok nótt is day-first (about 20 times in the saga corpora against 11 for nætr ok daga), and later Latin has die ac nocte. This fits reckoning time by nights, which ancient sources attribute to Germanic and Gaulish peoples. Caveats: a time merism is close to universal, and both ON slab texts are translated literature (Þiðreks saga; Barlaams saga for the unanchored context line in BC-58680). The slab's Greek anchors are prose and only partly congruent. Vedic mostly has dívā náktam, day first.
phrase: *nókʷt-(m̥/n̥s) ... + renewed 'day', adverbial accusative of extent: 'nights and days' = continuously (ON nætr ok daga, Gk νύκτας τε καὶ ἦμαρ, Lat. noctesque diesque, Ved. náktam ... dívā)

note: All 165 pivots are Early Modern Irish devotional/homiletic prose (CELT G100055/G100056, Keating-era), heavy with biblical translation. Partners are mostly Galen, Plutarch and Philo prose, with some ON/OHG prose and a little Sanskrit epic. Almost nothing congruent. One low-confidence claim: the night-first 'nights and days' merism (cognate night-word, renewed day-word), resting mainly on corpus support (Homer, sagas, Ennius/Lucretius, RV).
